contentHtml:
London: Only between a quarter and a third of people currently diagnosed with obesity should be considered as in poor health, according to a new study that joins calls to overhaul how the condition is diagnosed.The study, published in Nature on Wednesday, follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organizations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person's weight and height, to include body fat and broader health.

The study attempts to show what this new definition could mean for diagnosis levels, prevalence, and ultimately, treatment, for a condition the World Health Organization currently estimates affects more than one billion people globally.

Advt

Obesity can be a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease and cancer. The study suggests defining it as pre-clinical, when the condition is largely a risk factor, and clinical, when it is causing ill health.

WAIST CIRCUMFERENCE SHOULD BE PART OF DIAGNOSIS, STUDY SAYSUsing data from almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the study estimates that under the new framework, 1% to 3% of those defined as obese using BMI alone would not be, while another 5% to 9%, with higher body fat for example, would be diagnosed with the condition. Across a population, this could affect tens of millions of people.

The study's senior author Francesco Rubino, professor and chair of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King's College London, said the inaccuracy of BMI measurements was well-known."But we haven't so far got a better system," he said. That is what the new framework aims to do, he added, saying it could "provide a meaningful clinical characterization of obesity that can inform care and policy."

The new framework proposes measuring body fat, including by waist circumference, as well as BMI, and considering if a patient has any organ dysfunction linked to weight, like heart or liver problems, before making a diagnosis.

Advt

This means some people with high BMI alone would not be classed as having obesity. Those who have high body fat and high BMI would be diagnosed with "pre-clinical obesity", and those who also have organ dysfunction would have "clinical obesity" - considered an active disease that would usually require more urgent treatment.

Under these criteria, only on average roughly 27% of people with obesity across the four studied countries have clinical obesity, the study estimated - representing around 8.5% of all adults.The majority of those with "pre-clinical obesity" - around 82% on average across the four countries studied - did not progress to clinical obesity, although progression rates were higher in China and Spain, the study found.
